turns.prompt_text: How difficult would it be for me to design custom switch controllers? I imagine the electronics are the most difficult part and I imagine they use Bluetooth low energy
turns.response_html:
Designing a custom wireless Nintendo Switch controller is an excellent, highly achievable project, especially if you enjoy diving into custom hardware.

The overall difficulty sits right at medium-advanced. However, the division of labor isn't exactly where you might expect. The electronics layout is actually quite straightforward; the real nuances lie in the wireless protocol and the mechanical execution.

1. The Wireless Protocol: Bluetooth Classic vs. BLE

You hit right on the core challenge, but with a slight twist: The Nintendo Switch actually uses Bluetooth Classic (specifically Bluetooth HID), not Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE), for active gameplay. Because standard Bluetooth HID requires high-frequency reporting to minimize latency, it can be a bit more resource-intensive to program from scratch.

  • The Good News: You don't have to reverse-engineer it yourself. The Switch controller protocol has been thoroughly cracked by the maker community.
  • The Component Choice: An ESP32 is the gold standard for this project. There are robust, open-source firmware repositories (like the HOJA library or ESP32-Switch-Controller) that emulate a native Nintendo Switch Pro Controller flawlessly over Bluetooth. The Switch will recognize your custom hardware natively in the "Change Grip/Order" menu without needing any USB dongles.

2. Electronics Difficulty: Low to Medium

If you choose a micro-controller like an ESP32, the electronics are mostly repetitive.

[Buttons/Joysticks] ---> [GPIO Pins] ---> [ESP32] ---> (Bluetooth Classic) ---> [Nintendo Switch]
                                            ^
[LiPo Battery] --------> [TP4056 Charger] --+

The Circuit Architecture

Your PCB schematic will essentially consist of:

  • Input Routing: Standard tactile buttons or custom silicone membranes routed directly to the ESP32’s GPIO pins.
  • Analog Sticks: Standard 10k pots or modern Hall Effect joysticks tied to the ESP32’s Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) pins.
  • Power Delivery: A basic LiPo battery management circuit—typically a TP4056 charging IC coupled with a 3.3V voltage regulator to keep everything stable.

Designing this in a tool like KiCad and getting it manufactured via standard fab houses is an incredibly smooth pipeline. The trickiest part here is simply routing the traces cleanly around the physical constraints of your buttons.

3. Ergonomics & Mechanicals: The Silent Boss

While the electronics just need to work, the physical shell and buttons have to feel good, which is a surprisingly high hurdle.

  • Button Feel: 3D-printed buttons pressing directly onto tactile microswitches can feel loud, clicky, and rigid. Achieving that premium "console feel" usually requires sourcing original equipment manufacturer (OEM) conductive silicone membranes and designing a PCB that features matching carbon pads or gold-plated contact fingers.
  • Tolerances: Joysticks and triggers require incredibly tight mechanical tolerances. If your 3D-printed top shell is off by even 0.5mm, the analog sticks might rub against the edge, catch, or fail to hit their maximum values.

Using standard filaments like PLA or PETG for the rigid structural frame and prototyping with flexible filaments (TPU) for custom internal gaskets or dampeners is highly effective here.

Next Steps to Get Started

If you want to take this from concept to reality, I highly recommend a staged approach:

  1. Breadboard Prototype: Grab a standard ESP32 development board, wire up a couple of loose push-buttons on a breadboard, and flash an open-source Switch controller emulator script to confirm the wireless pairing behavior.
  2. Form Factor Design: Print a rough 3D mockup of your controller's shell to map out exactly where your hands rest before you finalize the physical shape of your PCB.

For an excellent deep dive into how an ESP32 handles this exact hardware emulation workflow, check out this DIY WIRELESS Nintendo Switch controller video. This clip showcases an arcade cabinet build using custom code to talk directly to the console over Bluetooth, which provides a fantastic roadmap for configuring your own firmware environment.
